text:
INVITATION TO TENDER
Patient portal for Brackenmoor NHS Foundation Trust
ITT reference BMT/2026/PP/07. Two-stage procurement under the Provider Selection Regime.
Clarification questions by 12 noon on 3 October. Responses by 12 noon on 24 October.

1. THE TRUST

Brackenmoor is a 400-bed acute trust with two hospital sites and eleven community clinics. We look after about 400,000 registered patients and ran 612,000 outpatient appointments last year. Our patient administration system is being replaced separately; this procurement is for the portal that patients themselves use.

2. THE PROBLEM

Our outpatient did-not-attend rate is 9.2%, which is 56,000 wasted appointments a year. When we ask patients why, the answer is almost never that they forgot: it is that the letter arrived after the appointment, or that they could not move a date that no longer worked, or that they did not know what the appointment was for. Meanwhile our booking office takes 4,100 calls a week and two thirds of those calls are a patient asking to move or confirm something they could do themselves in a minute.

We want a portal that lets a patient see and manage their own care, so that the phone lines are for the people who need them and clinical time is not spent on empty chairs. We are not trying to digitise everything. We are trying to remove the reasons people miss appointments.

3. WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE

  - 40% of eligible appointment changes done by patients themselves within twelve months of go-live.
  - Did-not-attend rate down from 9.2% to 7% or below across outpatients.
  - Calls to the booking office down by 25%.
  - 60,000 patients registered and 40,000 monthly active within a year.
  - No widening of inequality: uptake in the two most deprived deciles within five percentage points of the trust average. If a proposal cannot measure this, it does not meet the requirement.

4. WHO USES IT

  Patient - sees their own record, books where allowed, messages their team
  Carer or proxy - sees what the patient has consented to share, with an expiry
  Clinician - releases results and letters, answers clinical messages
  Booking team - creates and moves appointments the patient cannot move
  Records team - verifies identity, merges duplicates, fixes demographics
  Safeguarding lead - hides documents, suspends access, reviews proxy grants
  IT service desk - resets access, reads the audit log, cannot see clinical content

5. FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS

Mandatory unless marked. "The patient" means the person the record belongs to.

PR-001  A patient signs in with NHS login; anyone without one can register from inside the portal and come back.
PR-002  A patient who cannot use NHS login can be given a local account by the records team, with identity checked in person.
PR-003  A carer can be granted proxy access to another patient's record, with an expiry date and a written consent record.
PR-004  Proxy access is visible to the patient, who can revoke it themselves without phoning anybody.
PR-005  The home screen shows the next appointment, anything the patient must do before it, and unread messages.
PR-006  A patient can book, rebook or cancel an appointment in the clinics that allow self-booking.
PR-007  Clinics that do not allow self-booking show a request button that creates a task for the booking team instead.
PR-008  Rebooking respects the clinical rules set per clinic: minimum notice, maximum distance from the original date, and who may move a follow-up.
PR-009  A cancelled appointment releases the slot back to the booking system within one minute.
PR-010  Appointment reminders go out by SMS seven days and one day before, and by letter for patients with no mobile number.
PR-011  A patient can add the appointment to their own calendar and see how to get to the right building.
PR-012  The patient sees their clinic letters once the clinician has released them, not before.
PR-013  Test results are shown only after the responsible clinician releases them, with the clinician's plain-English comment attached.
PR-014  A patient can see their current medication list and request a repeat prescription from it.
PR-015  A repeat request is routed to the prescribing team and its status is visible to the patient at every step.
PR-016  A patient can complete a pre-appointment questionnaire on their phone, and the answers reach the clinician's worklist.
PR-017  Questionnaires are built by the clinical teams themselves from a library of question types, without a developer.
PR-018  A patient can upload a photograph of a wound or a rash when the clinic has asked for one.
PR-019  Secure messaging between a patient and a named team, with a stated response time and an out-of-hours notice.
PR-020  A message thread closes automatically after 30 days of silence and tells the patient how to reopen it.
PR-021  A patient can update their address, phone number and preferred contact method, which flows to the master record.
PR-022  Interpreter and accessibility needs are recorded once and travel with the patient to every clinic.
PR-023  The patient can nominate a preferred pharmacy for their prescriptions.
PR-024  Private patients can pay an invoice in the portal; NHS patients must never see a payment screen.
PR-025  Clinicians see a worklist of released results, questionnaire answers and messages awaiting a reply.
PR-026  A clinician can release a result with one click from the worklist, with an optional template comment.
PR-027  The records team can search for a patient by NHS number, name and date of birth, or hospital number.
PR-028  The records team can merge two duplicate patient records, with the merge written to the audit log and reversible for 24 hours.
PR-029  Every screen a staff member opens against a patient record is logged, including a read with no change.
PR-030  An administrator can suspend portal access for one patient immediately, for safeguarding reasons.
PR-031  Safeguarding flags hide named documents from the portal without telling the patient a document exists.
PR-032  A patient under 16 loses proxy access for their parent automatically on their sixteenth birthday, subject to local policy.
PR-033  Content (letters, questionnaires, help pages) is available in English and in the six languages the trust translates into.
PR-034  The portal reads and writes through the trust's FHIR R4 interface; nothing writes directly to the PAS database.
PR-035  Where the FHIR interface has no resource for something, the vendor proposes an extension and we agree it in writing.
PR-036  The portal degrades safely when the interface is down: it says so, and it never shows stale clinical data without a timestamp.
PR-037  An outage of the underlying systems must not lose a patient's questionnaire answers; they resume where they left off.
PR-038  Usage statistics by clinic, by age band and by deprivation decile, so we can see who the portal is not reaching.
PR-039  A digital inclusion report each month: how many patients could not complete a journey and where they stopped.

5.1 REQUIREMENTS ADDED AFTER THE ACCESSIBILITY RESEARCH IN APPENDIX C

PR-040  A patient can request hospital transport from the appointment screen where the clinic offers it.
PR-041  A patient can tell us they no longer need an appointment and say why, which goes to the clinic as a discharge request.
PR-042  The appointment screen shows the building, the floor, a map and how long to allow after arriving.
PR-043  Cancelling always offers the next available dates before it confirms the cancellation.
PR-044  A patient can ask for large print, easy read or a translated version of any letter, and the request is recorded once for all future letters.
PR-045  The portal never uses a clinical term where a plain one exists, and the words used are agreed with our reader panel.
PR-046  Every notification tells the patient what will happen next and when, not only that something has changed.
PR-047  A patient can show a check-in code on their phone at reception without printing anything.
PR-048  The messaging screen states the response time and what to do instead in an emergency, above the message box, not below it.
PR-049  Anything that fails for a patient (a timeout, a rejected upload) is logged with enough detail for us to find the patient and help them.

6. NON-FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS

NFR-01  WCAG 2.2 AA for every patient-facing screen, tested with real assistive technology users, not only with an automated tool.
NFR-02  The portal must work on a five-year-old Android phone on a 3G connection in a rural area.
NFR-03  99.9% availability between 06:00 and 22:00, and 99.5% overnight, measured monthly.
NFR-04  A page must render in under three seconds at the 95th percentile on the connection described above.
NFR-05  All data stays in the United Kingdom, including backups, logs and anything a support engineer can see.
NFR-06  NHS Data Security and Protection Toolkit standards met before go-live and reassessed every year.
NFR-07  DCB0129 clinical risk management: a clinical safety case and a hazard log, signed by our clinical safety officer.
NFR-08  Information governance: role-based access, break-glass with justification, and an immutable audit trail.
NFR-09  Clinical audit records kept for eight years after the last entry, in line with the records management code.
NFR-10  Penetration testing before go-live and annually, by a CHECK-accredited supplier, with findings fixed to an agreed timetable.
NFR-11  No third-party analytics or advertising trackers of any kind on patient-facing pages.
NFR-12  Support for 400,000 registered patients, 40,000 monthly active users and 3,000 concurrent sessions on a Monday morning.
NFR-13  Planned maintenance only between 23:00 and 05:00, announced a week ahead inside the portal.
NFR-14  Disaster recovery: a four-hour recovery time objective and a 15-minute recovery point objective, tested annually with us watching.

7. INTEGRATION AND TECHNICAL CONSTRAINTS

The portal integrates through our integration engine over HL7 FHIR R4. It must not read or write the patient administration system directly, and it must not hold a clinical record of its own: anything clinical is a view of the source system, fetched live or cached with a visible timestamp.

Authentication for patients is NHS login at NHS login level of confidence P9 for anything clinical. Staff authenticate through the trust's Microsoft Entra ID with conditional access; smartcard authentication is not required for this portal.

Hosting must be in a UK region of a major cloud provider, in the vendor's tenancy, with the trust holding a right to audit. Our infrastructure team runs nothing for you and will not accept an appliance in our data centre.

The FHIR resources we expose today:

  Patient - demographics, NHS number, contact preferences, interpreter need
  RelatedPerson - carers and proxies, with the consent that granted access
  Appointment and Schedule - slots, clinic rules, cancellations
  Encounter - the visit itself, for the history the patient sees
  DocumentReference - clinic letters and discharge summaries
  DiagnosticReport and Observation - results, with the release status we add as an extension
  MedicationRequest - the repeat list and the status of a new request
  Questionnaire and QuestionnaireResponse - pre-appointment forms
  Communication - secure messages, so they live in the record and not only in the portal
  Consent - proxy access, research contact, and data sharing preferences
  AuditEvent - every read and write, exported nightly to the trust SIEM

SMS is sent through the trust's existing gateway contract; the vendor must use it rather than bringing their own. Letters are printed by our existing print and post supplier, and the portal only suppresses a letter when the patient has opted out.

8. WHAT IS OUT OF SCOPE

Video consultation, which we buy elsewhere. Inpatient discharge workflow. Anything that writes a clinical note. A native mobile app: we want the web to work well on a phone, and we will revisit an app when the web version is proven.

9. IMPLEMENTATION AND TIMETABLE

  Contract award                                       January
  Discovery with two clinical teams                    February to March
  Private beta, one outpatient clinic, 500 patients    May
  Public beta, five clinics, 20,000 patients           July
  Trust-wide go-live                                   Quarter three, and no later than 30 September
  Letters and results in all clinics                   Quarter four
  Decommission the old appointment reminder service    December

Go-live cannot slip past 30 September because the reminder contract it replaces ends then.

10. COMMERCIALS

We are not publishing a budget for this procurement. Price on the basis of the requirements above, broken down into implementation, annual licence and support, and a day rate for change requests. Bidders who ask us to name a figure in clarification will be answered with this paragraph.

11. EVALUATION

60% quality, 30% price, 10% social value. Within quality: clinical safety and information governance 20%, accessibility and digital inclusion 20%, integration approach 10%, delivery plan 10%. A proposal that fails the accessibility requirement is not scored further.

12. APPENDIX B - CLINICS, VOLUMES AND BOOKING RULES

13. APPENDIX C - WHAT THE ACCESSIBILITY RESEARCH FOUND

Fourteen patients, recruited through our reader panel and two community groups, tried our current letters and a prototype in June. The findings below are requirements in everything but name.

F01. Eleven of fourteen participants over 70 could not complete registration without help, and all eleven stopped at the identity check rather than at the login itself.

F02. Three participants using a screen reader lost their place in the appointment list because the filter re-rendered the page without announcing it.

F03. Two participants with low vision could not read the appointment time against the background colour our current letters use.

F04. Participants did not understand the phrase clinic letter; they called it my letter from the hospital.

F05. Everyone asked where the appointment was before they asked when it was, and nobody found the building name useful without a map.

F06. Four participants expected cancelling to offer an alternative date immediately, and read a plain confirmation as the appointment being lost.

F07. Two carers were sharing the patient's own login because proxy access was too hard to set up. Both knew it was wrong and did it anyway.

F08. Participants with English as a second language used the browser translation and got clinical terms wrong in both directions.

F09. Nobody read the out-of-hours notice on the messaging screen; two sent an urgent message on a Friday evening expecting a reply.

F10. Six of fourteen participants had no working printer and needed a way to show the appointment on the phone at reception.

14. APPENDIX D - GLOSSARY

DNA - did not attend, a booked appointment the patient did not come to.
PAS - patient administration system, the source of appointments and demographics.
FHIR - the interoperability standard our integration engine speaks.
Proxy - a carer or relative acting for a patient with recorded consent.
Break-glass - emergency access to a record outside a user's normal permissions, always audited.
DSPT - the NHS Data Security and Protection Toolkit.
DCB0129 - the clinical risk management standard for health software manufacturers.
Deprivation decile - a measure of how deprived a patient's area is; we report uptake against it.

15. APPENDIX E - WHAT THE BOOKING OFFICE IS CALLED ABOUT

A week of calls, sampled in June, coded by our own staff. The first five lines are 71% of the volume and are the ones the portal has to absorb.

  Move an appointment to a different date                    1,180 calls
  Confirm an appointment the patient is unsure about           720 calls
  Ask what an appointment is for                               430 calls
  Cancel an appointment                                        390 calls
  Ask where to go and where to park                            190 calls
  Chase a letter that has not arrived                          185 calls
  Ask for a result                                             170 calls
  Change a phone number or an address                          160 calls
  Ask for transport                                            145 calls
  Ask for an interpreter                                        95 calls
  Ask about a repeat prescription                               90 calls
  Report that the patient has died                              55 calls
  Ask for a letter in large print or another language           45 calls
  Complain about a previous call                                40 calls
  Everything else                                              205 calls

The last four lines are in the table so that nobody proposes removing the phone number from the website. Some of these calls must stay calls.

16. APPENDIX F - THINGS THE PORTAL MUST NEVER SHOW

  A result that the responsible clinician has not released, in any view, including a partial list or a count.
  A document flagged by safeguarding, including any hint that a document exists.
  Another patient's data, including in a shared household where two patients use the same device.
  A free-text clinical note written for colleagues rather than for the patient.
  An appointment for a service the patient has asked us not to show, such as sexual health or termination of pregnancy.
  A diagnosis in an SMS or a push notification, however convenient it would be.
  A staff member's personal contact details, including a direct mobile number in a letter template.
notes: Over 20k characters and deliberately budget-free: section 10 refuses to name a figure, so P-07 is MISSING even though everything else is PRESENT. A model that infers a budget from the size of the trust has invented it.
